body: Peruvian licence plates can be white or yellow; yellow plates are less common and typically used for taxis with yellow top and white bottom. Yellow plates in South America are mainly found in Peru, Colombia, and rarely Chile.
Generation 3 coverage features a black and white Google car; black cars appear only in Peru, Argentina, and Uruguay, while white cars appear in Peru, Bolivia, and Chile.
Peru has Generation 4 Street View coverage, unlike Bolivia; Ecuador has some Generation 4 coverage but always with a large pickup truck.
Peru and Brazil are the only South American countries with Generation 4 smallcam coverage, mounted lower with a circular blur and front protrusion.

Peruvian roads have white outer lines. Highways have either single yellow dashed or double yellow middle lines. Rural mountain roads mostly have white outer lines without centre lines. Divided highways may have completely white lines. These mountain road features are mostly found in Peru.
Peru uses black-and-white striped signposts and sometimes black-and-yellow signposts, uniquely in South America.
Peru predominantly uses triangular-shaped concrete bollards painted red or yellow, with occasional circular concrete variants.
Guardrails throughout Peru have black-and-yellow stripes, sometimes with sharp arrow designs. Peru uses outer black stripes, while Bolivia uses yellow.
Kilometre markers in Peru are concrete painted black and white, occasionally showing road numbers near urban areas.
Peruvian metal signposts stand on concrete blocks, unique in South America.
Poles vary between concrete and wood; some have horizontal concrete bars like Argentina.
Some poles have painted black or black-and-yellow bottoms, distinctive to Peru but similar to Colombia’s patterns.
Bridges in Peru commonly feature orange paint.
Peru mainly comprises semi-arid mountain ranges and valleys.
Tuk tuks (mototaxis) are seen frequently in major cities including Lima, Trujillo, Chiclayo, Piura, and Iquitos.
Wide red and white stickers are often attached to taxis and commercial vehicles.
The Peruvian currency, the Sol (S/.), is unique and occasionally visible in Street View.
Peru hosts many political party logos unique to the country.
Architecture includes Colonial-era, contemporary boxy buildings, and traditional red brick structures.
Street View coverage focuses on the west and main highways; some eastern exceptions near Iquitos and the 30C highway.
Peru’s terrain is flat in the east and mountainous in the west, with a flat desert near Piura in the northwest.
The country has a dry desert climate in the west and tropical rainforest in the east.
Highway numbers increase north to south; highways 1, 3, and 5 are longest and cross multiple departments.
Tumbes features sandy soil with green or withered bushes, without black cars on off roads.
Southwestern Piura is dry and flat with sparse vegetation, sometimes rolling hills.
Northwest Piura resembles the southwest but is noticeably hillier.
Coconut palms occur mainly in coastal areas north of Lima, particularly in agricultural zones near coastal cities.
Olive plantations are located in the southern Tacna region.
Sugar cane fields dominate northern coastal regions near Chiclayo and Trujillo, with smaller fields further south.
Banana plants are common adjacent to coastal agricultural northern regions.
Central Puno and Lake Chinchaycocha feature typically flat mountainous terrain similar to Bolivia, requiring additional clues for correct identification.
The region south of Lake Titicaca in eastern Peru shows low grass, small hills, stone village walls, and brown brick buildings.
Northern Peru has shrubby and bushy mountains often dry near the coast and the Ecuador border.
Pine plantations appear at higher elevations, mostly consisting of Pinus radiata and Pinus patula.
Areas near northern Amazonian city Tarapoto have moderately tall foliage-covered mountains similar to Colombia or Brazil.
Exposed rocky outcroppings are common in high elevations near Lago Chinchaycocha to Ayacucho; rare elsewhere in Peru.
Taller mountainous areas near central Peru have rocky, sharp tops stretching from Huaraz to Cusco.
Light green lichen grows on rocks and ground in central and southern high elevation areas.
Dark red soil is found near Cusco, Ayacucho, Cajamarca, and Tarapoto, with lesser presence in adjacent regions.
Barren, flat desert areas near Ica, Arequipa, and Tacna resemble northern Chile, with mountains often visible to the east.
Coastal agricultural valleys in mid and southern Peru lie between dry, non-vegetated mountains running southwest to northeast.
Red brick buildings are common closer to Lake Titicaca and resemble western Bolivia; blue-tinted glass is also common here.
Northern Peru mostly has overhanging roofs with wooden supports; some buildings are brightly coloured.
Open-fronted tuk-tuks are mostly found in northern Peru, especially near Amazonian regions.
A unique cylindrical bollard with black-and-yellow stripes is found only in Moquegua, in southern Peru.
The 1N highway near Piura and Lambayeque passes semidesert landscape with overcast Generation 3 coverage; Generation 4 is drier but similar.
Highway 1N/S is divided in the highlighted area; it is the only divided highway outside cities.
The 1S south of Ica is not divided, follows the coast with red or orange soil and little vegetation, covered entirely by Generation 4.
Route 5N between San Alejandro and Esperanza is a straight, flat path through rainforest.
Ruta 30C in eastern Peru has a dense forest with few villages resembling Brazil’s interior, mostly north-south and partly updated to Generation 4.
Ruta 28B between Kimbiri and Echarate is a small, paved, riverside road with faded or missing line markings and Generation 4 coverage.
The Jauja-Huancayo valley has a flat plain with trees, agriculture, villages, and north-south mountains on both sides.
The north side of Lake Titicaca was covered in a wetter season than the south side.
Lake Chinchaycocha north of Huancayo is marshy with nearby mountain ranges; less populated and tree-dense than Lake Titicaca.
Volcanoes occur mainly in the southeast near Arequipa.
Lima has many long, straight boulevard streets divided by concrete or grassy berms.
Pucallpa city near Brazil has a consistent WSW-ENE street grid with varied orientations in northern and eastern parts.
Iquitos in northeast Peru has Generation 3 coverage with three-wheeled tuk-tuks, overcast skies, and rolling Amazonian landscapes; isolated from northern Peru.
Cusco features a mix of red brick and Spanish colonial buildings surrounded by mountains with a central airport; it resembles La Paz, Bolivia.
Tacna city in southern Peru has a distinct dry ridge to the north.
A white Street View car operates between Aguas Calientes and Machu Picchu in central Cusco.
A train track covered by a trekker is located between Aguas Calientes and Cusco.
